params.text: The quiet return of local-first software

For a decade, the default answer to every software question was the cloud. Notes, documents and even voices lived on someone else's server, rented back to us by the month. Lately that answer has started to wobble. Small models now run on an ordinary laptop, and they sound good enough that nobody asks where the audio came from.

The appeal is simple. When the work happens on your own machine, it keeps working on a plane, in a tunnel, and long after a startup has changed its pricing. Nothing leaves the device, so there is nothing to leak. Speed stops depending on a data centre three time zones away.
None of this is nostalgia. It is a bet that the best software is the kind that disappears into the task, and that it can only do so when it is fast, private and yours to keep.

Three things changed at once. Phones and laptops gained dedicated silicon for machine learning, open models shrank by an order of magnitude, and the tools to ship them became ordinary packages instead of research projects.
The result is software that treats the network as an optional extra. Sync still matters, but it happens when it can, not when it must, and the app never waits on a server to be useful.

params.text: Local-first does not mean offline-only. Sync still happens, but as a convenience layered on top of files you already hold, rather than a gate you must pass to reach your own work.
The trade is real. Updates are your job to ship, and a model that fits on a laptop will never match the largest one in a data centre. For reading text aloud, almost nobody can tell the difference.
The next decade of software may be defined less by what it adds than by what it no longer asks of us: an account, a connection, a subscription.

Whether that vision wins will not be decided by benchmarks. It will be decided by small, ordinary moments: the tool that opens instantly on a train, the document that is still there next year, the voice that never asks you to sign in.
That is the quiet part. Nobody announces it. One day a person notices that nothing they rely on needs permission from a server, and wonders why it was ever different.
